Hierarchical Long-Term Semantic Memory for LinkedIn’s Hiring Agent

CCS: Computing methodologies Natural language processingCCS: Computing methodologies Knowledge representation and reasoningCCS: Information systems Information retrievalCCS: Information systems Data management systems
Zhentao Xu email: zhexu@linkedin.com Affiliation: LinkedIn Corporation, Sunnyvale, CA, USA , Shangjing Zhang email: shanzhang@linkedin.com Affiliation: LinkedIn Corporation, Sunnyvale, CA, USA , Emir Poyraz email: epoyraz@linkedin.com Affiliation: LinkedIn Corporation, Sunnyvale, CA, USA , Yvonne Li email: yiwli@linkedin.com Affiliation: LinkedIn Corporation, Sunnyvale, CA, USA , Ye Jin email: yejin@linkedin.com Affiliation: LinkedIn Corporation, Sunnyvale, CA, USA , Xie Lu email: xilu@linkedin.com Affiliation: LinkedIn Corporation, Sunnyvale, CA, USA , Xiaoyang Gu email: xgu@linkedin.com Affiliation: LinkedIn Corporation, Sunnyvale, CA, USA , Karthik Ramgopal email: kramgopa@linkedin.com Affiliation: LinkedIn Corporation, Sunnyvale, CA, USA , Praveen Kumar Bodigutla email: pbodigutla@linkedin.com Affiliation: LinkedIn Corporation, Sunnyvale, CA, USA, 94085 and Xiaofeng Wang email: xiaofwang@linkedin.com Affiliation: LinkedIn Corporation, Sunnyvale, CA, USA, 94085
2026
Abstract.

Large Language Model (LLM) agents are increasingly used in real-world products, where personalized and context-aware user interactions are essential. A central enabler of such capabilities is the agent’s long-term semantic memory system, which extracts implicit and explicit signals from noisy longitudinal behavioral data, stores them in a structured form, and supports low-latency retrieval. Building industrial-grade long-term memory for LLM agents raises five challenges: scalability, low-latency retrieval, privacy constraints, cross-domain generalizability, and observability. We introduce the Hierarchical Long-Term Semantic Memory (HLTM) framework, which organizes textual data into a schema-aligned memory tree that captures semantic knowledge at multiple levels of granularity, enabling scalable ingestion, privacy-aware storage, low-latency retrieval, and transparent provenance; HLTM further incorporates an adaptation mechanism to generalize across diverse use cases. Extensive evaluations on LinkedIn’s Hiring Assistant show that HLTM improves answer correctness and retrieval F1 significantly by more than 10%11 1 Disclaimer: Results may vary in production environments or with different datasets, while significantly advancing the Pareto frontier between query and indexing latency. HLTM has been deployed in LinkedIn’s Hiring Assistant to power core personalization features in production hiring workflows.

Keywords: 
LLM agents, long-term semantic memory, agent memory, hierarchical memory, retrieval-augmented generation

1. Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) such as GPT (Achiam et al., 2023), Claude (Anthropic, 2025), and Gemini (Comanici et al., 2025) have demonstrated strong performance across a wide range of tasks in real-world agent systems, including question answering, code generation, and retrieval-augmented search (Kamalloo et al., 2023; Zan et al., 2023; Zhu et al., 2025). Modern LLM-based agents (Wang et al., 2024) augment these models with external tools (Schick et al., 2023) and carefully designed workflows to enhance their reasoning and planning capabilities (Wei et al., 2022; Yao et al., 2023). For example, LinkedIn’s Hiring Assistant (LiHA) (Gu et al., 2025) is an AI recruiting agent that helps recruiters source, evaluate, and outreach to candidates at scale. Agentic memory systems (Zhang et al., 2025b; Zhong et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025a; Xu et al., 2025; Jimenez Gutierrez et al., 2024; Chhikara et al., 2025) support an agent’s long-term interaction with its environment while maintaining continuity over time. They enable agents to persist user-specific signals from historical data and interactions and to leverage them to personalize future agent–user exchanges. For instance, LiHA (Gu et al., 2025) needs to extract personalized hiring preferences from recruiters’ past projects and activities, and to recall and reason over this recruiter-specific memory to generate tailored, contextually appropriate responses in future interactions. Achieving this level of personalization at scale requires a memory system that can reliably extract implicit and explicit signals from noisy longitudinal behavioral data, store them in a structured form, and retrieve them efficiently during real-time conversations.

Recent work has advanced agents’ long-context capabilities by introducing explicit memory modules. Systems such as MemGPT, Mem0, MemoryBank, ReadAgent, SimpleMem, and SCM (Packer et al., 2023; Chhikara et al., 2025; Zhong et al., 2024; Lee et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2023) extend LLMs with external stores that swap, persist, and selectively retrieve interaction traces beyond the native context window. Complementary efforts explore more structured representations: GraphRAG, HippoRAG, A-Mem, and G-Memory (Edge et al., 2024; Jimenez Gutierrez et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025a) organize knowledge into graphs to support multi-hop reasoning, while RAPTOR, TreeRAG, and MemTree (Sarthi et al., 2024; Tao et al., 2025; Rezazadeh et al., 2024) exploit hierarchical structure for scalable long-context retrieval. Despite these advances, designing long-term semantic memory for large-scale, industrial-grade agents remains challenging across several key dimensions:

  • •

    Challenge 1: Industrial-scale Data Ingestion A production memory system must ingest and process large-scale structured or unstructured data from diverse sources and formats. This demands compact memory representations, highly parallelizable ingestion pipelines, and lossless incremental updates.

  • •

    Challenge 2: Low-latency Retrieval Many scenarios impose strict latency constraints. For example, chat-based agents must respond within tight budgets to maintain a fluent conversation, leaving little room for expensive retrieval or oversized context windows at serving time. As a result, most computation is ideally amortized offline or nearline, with only a lean, predictable retrieval path online.

  • •

    Challenge 3: Privacy-aware Memory Isolation Enterprise agents must comply with strict data-governance policies (e.g., GDPR (GDPR.eu, )). With these policies, the memory must enforce strict isolation, preventing cross-tenant retrieval, and support clean deletion when required.

  • •

    Challenge 4: Adaptability and Generality The memory framework should be generic enough to support multiple products and use cases, yet adaptive enough to incorporate new query patterns and evolving schemas without relying on brittle, hand-crafted business rules or per-feature pipelines.

  • •

    Challenge 5: Observability, Provenance, and Consistency under source-of-truth updates The memory system should preserve references to its underlying information sources and surface them during retrieval, enabling inspection, debugging, and governance. It should also remain consistent as the source of truth (SOT) evolves (e.g., edits, backfills, or deletions), preventing stale or contradictory memories.

To address these challenges, we propose HLTM, a hierarchical long-term semantic memory framework for industrial LLM agents. HLTM organizes memory into a tree-structured index that supports massively parallel execution and lossless incremental ingestion, generate multi-granularity memory representations for low-latency retrieval at serving time, and supports enhanced privacy policies by aligning the memory hierarchy with business scopes such as seats and projects. The framework remains general and adaptable through automatic query pattern analysis and adaptive knowledge extraction. Each memory node is bound to a stable business identifier, providing explicit provenance and observability for inspection, debugging, and governance. HLTM has been deployed as the long-term semantic memory component of LinkedIn’s Hiring Assistant (Gu et al., 2025) (Figure 1) and demonstrates robust, enterprise-scale performance (Figure 2).

Our main contributions are summarized below:

  • •

    Production-scale long-term memory for enterprise agents: We present an industrial-scale memory architecture that scales to millions of documents and supports lossless incremental updates. The system is deployed in LinkedIn’s Hiring Assistant and serves production hiring workflows.

  • •

    Hierarchical, tree-based memory representation: We propose a tree-structured memory topology with multi-view memory representation, enabling massively parallel indexing, privacy-preserving retrieval scoping, and low-latency serving.

  • •

    Adaptive ingestion via workload feedback: We design a lightweight adaptation loop that mines historical query patterns to continuously refine memory content and improve retrieval quality and efficiency.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews related research and industrial practices in agent memory. Section 3 presents the design and methodology of HLTM. Section 4 provides a comparative evaluation against existing memory techniques. Section 5 describes HLTM’s production use case in LinkedIn’s Hiring Assistant. Finally, Section 6 concludes the paper and outlines directions for future work.

2. Related Work

Recent work has substantially improved agents’ long-context processing by introducing explicit memory mechanisms. MemGPT (Packer et al., 2023) adopts an OS-inspired design that swaps information between the limited context window and external memory. Mem0 (Chhikara et al., 2025) stores discrete memory items and retrieves them primarily via semantic search. MemoryBank (Zhong et al., 2024) maintains timestamped interaction memories with time-based decay to emphasize recency and salience. ReadAgent (Lee et al., 2024) compresses long documents into compact gist memories with on-demand lookup of supporting passages. SCM (Wang et al., 2023) equips agents with a controller that adaptively decides when to store, update, or retrieve from a stream of past interactions.

Beyond unstructured memory stores, recent studies explore structured representations to improve organization and retrieval. GraphRAG (Edge et al., 2024) builds a knowledge graph and leverages community-based summarization to better capture entity-centric dependencies. HippoRAG (Jimenez Gutierrez et al., 2024) draws inspiration from hippocampal indexing, integrating graph-based retrieval with personalized PageRank for multi-hop reasoning and continual knowledge integration. A-mem (Xu et al., 2025) uses Zettelkasten-style atomic notes with dynamic linking to support autonomous memory evolution, while G-Memory (Zhang et al., 2025a) generalizes this direction to multi-agent settings with hierarchical graph structures that model both reusable insights and collaboration trajectories. In parallel, RAPTOR (Sarthi et al., 2024) and TreeRAG (Tao et al., 2025) leverage hierarchical structures for long-context retrieval, combining multi-level organization with structure-aware access to improve downstream QA. MemTree (Rezazadeh et al., 2024) complements this line with an incrementally updated memory tree that maintains node-level summaries and embeddings as agent knowledge evolves.

Despite these advances, enterprise deployment remains challenging. Many methods lack principled memory partitioning aligned with access boundaries, raising privacy and scope-isolation risks. Graph-based approaches often require extensive LLM usage during indexing and incur online latency, limiting scalability (Zhao et al., 2025). Tree-style methods frequently depend on the LLM’s world knowledge for aggregation, which can weaken domain-specific controllability (Maynez et al., 2020). Finally, most systems lack robust citation practices and provenance tracking, reducing transparency and debuggability in production (Cheng et al., 2025).

3. Method

3.1. Overview

We propose HLTM, a hierarchical long-term semantic memory that organizes information in a tree: higher-level nodes capture broad patterns, while lower-level nodes store fine-grained, entity-specific information. Together, these levels support both generic and highly targeted queries within a unified structure (Figure 3). In production, the tree topology aligns with business scope and access-control boundaries, enabling privacy enforcement by restricting retrieval to appropriate subtrees (Section 3.2). Node contents are built offline via data-driven preference extraction and hierarchical aggregation (Sections 3.3–3.4), and are queried at serving time using hybrid embedding-based retrieval and answered via in-context learning (Section 3.5). HLTM also supports adaptation to evolving query patterns and lossless incremental updates, enabling nearline freshness at low indexing cost (Sections 3.6–3.7).

3.2. Schema-aligned Hierarchical Topology

Most hierarchical memory systems adopt semantic hierarchies, clustering embeddings of text segments into progressively coarser nodes (Sarthi et al., 2024; Tao et al., 2025). While effective for organizing free-form text, this approach is ill-suited to multi-tenant enterprise privacy requirements: clustering can mix content across business scopes, creating privacy and compliance risks under strict isolation and access-control policies (Zeng et al., 2024; Jiang et al., 2024). Semantic hierarchies are also brittle under incremental updates: new data often triggers re-clustering and topology changes, while keeping the topology fixed can lead to quality drift and periodic full re-indexing.

Hierarchical schemas are ubiquitous in enterprise data (ownership chains), documents (structural nesting), and conversations (sessions and messages). HLTM exploits this by constructing a schema-aligned hierarchy whose topology is dictated by the enterprise data model and ownership boundaries. In the hiring domain, for example, leaf nodes represent fine-grained work units (e.g., hiring projects), intermediate nodes represent recruiter seats, and root nodes represent organizational accounts. We formalize this as a tree index 𝒯=(𝒱,ℰ)\mathcal{T}=(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E}), where 𝒱\mathcal{V} contains business entities and edges ℰ\mathcal{E} follow schema-defined parent–child relations. Each node v∈𝒱v\in\mathcal{V} owns the memory for its entity, and retrieval is restricted to subtrees consistent with the query scope and access-control policy.

This schema-aligned design provides three deployment-critical benefits: (i) privacy-aware scoping via subtree-restricted retrieval, enabling per-entity isolation and controlled sharing; (ii) localized incremental updates that touch only affected leaves and their ancestor nodes, reducing update cost from O⁡(|𝒱|)O(|\mathcal{V}|) to the tree height; and (iii) topology stability over time, avoiding drift and periodic full re-indexing commonly seen in clustering-based hierarchies.

3.3. Memory Representation

Rather than storing raw data at each node, we transform node content DvD_{v} for node v∈𝒱v\in\mathcal{V} into a compact, multi-view memory representation MvM_{v}:

Mv=(Fv,Qv,Sv)M_{v}=\big(F_{v},Q_{v},S_{v}\big)

where SvS_{v}, FvF_{v}, and QvQ_{v} denote the summary, facet, and QA views at node v∈𝒱v\in\mathcal{V}, respectively. The full prompt templates for the three agents are provided in Appendix A.

  • •

    Facet (Key–Value) Representation. Key–value pairs provide a structured and interpretable view of salient facts, making them easy to index, filter, and retrieve. We prompt an LLM to extract a set of facet pairs Fv={(key,value)}F_{v}=\{(\mathrm{key},\mathrm{value})\} from DvD_{v} and store them in a document database. To support semantic retrieval, we linearize each pair (e.g., location: SF Bay Area) and compute an embedding for indexing.

  • •

    Answerable-QA Representation. Question–answer pairs align with how users naturally phrase queries, so embedded questions often lie closer to user queries in embedding space, improving retrieval accuracy. They also enable a “think-fast” serving mode by precomputing answerable questions offline, minimizing online computation. Concretely, we prompt an LLM to generate answerable QA pairs Qv={(q,a)}Q_{v}=\{(q,a)\} from the raw data DvD_{v} and store them in a document database. To support semantic retrieval, we embed and index each question in a vector store.

  • •

    Summary Representation. Some knowledge is inherently unstructured (e.g., nuanced narratives or multi-step logic) and is not naturally captured by key–value or QA formats; therefore, we use natural-language summarization as the default representation. Specifically, we prompt an LLM to first compress DvD_{v} into a detailed paragraph SvS_{v} that preserves key information, and then distill it into a single-sentence summary to compute embeddings for vector-store indexing.

3.4. Hierarchical Memory Aggregation

Summarization-style queries that ask for a summary or synthesis over a broad scope typically require aggregating evidence from multiple leaf nodes (Edge et al., 2024). A straightforward strategy is to retrieve a large set of relevant leaf-level documents at query time and ask the LLM to summarize them on the fly; however, this approach is often impractical for three reasons: (i) high online cost, because summarizing detail-heavy evidence is both token-intensive and latency-critical; (ii) the needle-in-a-haystack effect, where relevant signals are drowned out by irrelevant details, increasing the likelihood of omissions and factual drift; and (iii) embedding-space misalignment, where broad summarization queries may not align well with leaf-level embeddings, leading to poor recall and unstable retrieval quality.

To address these challenges, HLTM performs offline hierarchical aggregation, composing child memories into broader-scope parent representations in a bottom-up manner. Aggregation follows the parent–child relations defined by the tree topology (Section 3.2) and is applied recursively up to the root. For each parent node p∈𝒱p\in\mathcal{V}, we collect its children’s memory representations {Mc}\{M_{c}\} as input and prompt an LLM agent to generate parent-level representations in the same multi-view form. Specifically, we guide the LLM to (i) group semantically similar evidence across children, (ii) merge redundant content and reconcile conflicts, and (iii) optionally prune low-salience details that rarely recur across children.

3.5. Memory Retrieval and Answer Generation

HLTM performs identity-scoped multi-signal retrieval to efficiently retrieve privacy-compliant memory content for a given user query. Building on RAPTOR’s collapsed-tree paradigm (Sarthi et al., 2024), which collapses nodes across levels into a single candidate pool for retrieval, we introduce two production-critical extensions: (i) identity-scoped subtree filtering to enforce enterprise access boundaries, and (ii) multi-signal retrieval to robustly surface relevant memories under diverse query formulations.

3.5.1. Identity-scoped Subtree Filtering

Each production query is issued under an explicit identity scope that maps to a node vv in our schema-aligned hierarchy (Section 3.2). We enforce this scope via hard filtering: retrieval candidates are restricted to the subtree 𝒯v\mathcal{T}_{v} rooted at node vv, guaranteeing strict tenant isolation. For example, a recruiter-scoped query may access only the recruiter node and its descendants; nodes owned by other recruiters are excluded. Formally,

𝒯v=𝒯⁡[{v}∪Desc⁡(v)]\mathcal{T}_{v}=\mathcal{T}\big[\{v\}\cup\mathrm{Desc}(v)\big]

3.5.2. Multi-signal Retrieval

Within the privacy-scoped subtree 𝒯v\mathcal{T}_{v}, we build on RAPTOR’s collapsed-tree retrieval method (Sarthi et al., 2024) and extend it with multi-retriever scoring. Rather than relying on a single similarity signal, we rank candidates using three complementary retrievers tied to the node representations in Section 3.3: the facet-based retriever capturing structured constraints, the answerable-QA retriever capturing query-like intents, and the summary-based retriever capturing free-form semantics. Each retriever produces a relevance score, and we return the top-kk memories per view as retrieval context.

  • •

    Facet-based Retrieval: We enable fine-grained, schema-aware matching by parsing the query qq into a set of facet key–value pairs FqF_{q}. Each pair is then linearized into a micro-query (“key: val\mathrm{val}”) and compared against the offline-constructed facet strings in FvF_{v} for each node vv in embedding space. For example, the query ‘‘typical workplace for hiring software engineers in the San Francisco Bay Area?’’ is decomposed into two micro-queries: ‘‘title: software engineer’’ and ‘‘location: San Francisco Bay Area’’. We aggregate similarities into a query–node score sfacet​(q,v)s_{\text{facet}}(q,v) and return the facet sets Fk​(q)F_{k}(q) from the top-kfacetk_{\text{facet}} nodes.

    sfacet​(q,v)=1|Fq|​|Fv|​∑f∈Fq∑f′∈Fvcos⁡(emb⁡(f),emb⁡(f′))s_{\text{facet}}(q,v)=\frac{1}{|F_{q}|\,|F_{v}|}\sum_{f\in F_{q}}\sum_{f^{\prime}\in F_{v}}\cos\,\bigl(\mathrm{emb}(f),\mathrm{emb}(f^{\prime})\bigr)
  • •

    Answerable-QA Retrieval: We match the query qq against a node’s offline-generated answerable question set QvQ_{v}. Specifically, we embed qq and each q′∈Qvq^{\prime}\in Q_{v}, compute cosine similarities, and score node vv by the best-matching question sQA​(q,v)s_{\text{QA}}(q,v). We then return the top-kQAk_{\text{QA}} answerable question–answer pairs Qk​(q)Q_{k}(q).

    sQA​(q,v)=maxq′∈Qv⁡cos⁡(emb⁡(q),emb⁡(q′))s_{\text{QA}}(q,v)=\max_{q^{\prime}\in Q_{v}}\cos\,\bigl(\mathrm{emb}(q),\,\mathrm{emb}(q^{\prime})\bigr)
  • •

    Summary-based Retrieval: We embed the query qq and each node’s offline-generated summary view SvS_{v}, rank nodes by cosine similarity, and return the top-ksummaryk_{\text{summary}} summaries Sk​(q)S_{k}(q).

    ssummary​(q,v)=cos⁡(emb⁡(q),emb⁡(Sv))s_{\text{summary}}(q,v)=\cos\,\bigl(\mathrm{emb}(q),\,\mathrm{emb}(S_{v})\bigr)

3.5.3. Answer Generation with Retrieved Context

After retrieval, we apply a standard in-context learning prompt that conditions the LLM on the top-ranked memory contents as context. In addition to the final answer, the system also returns references, namely the IDs of the retrieved memory tree nodes used as grounding evidence (Figure 1), enabling provenance tracking and downstream inspection. The prompt template is provided in Appendix B.2.

answer,references=LLM⁡(q,Fk​(q)∪Qk​(q)∪Sk​(q))\mathrm{answer},\mathrm{references}=\mathrm{LLM}\bigl(q,\,F_{k}(q)\cup Q_{k}(q)\cup S_{k}(q)\bigr)

3.6. Adaptation via Query Pattern Analysis

To remain adaptive under continuously shifting production query patterns and an evolving document corpus, we introduce a periodic adaptation step that distills historical query workloads into signals for memory construction, rather than relying solely on an LLM’s world knowledge to determine what is important to memorize. Over a sliding window of past queries, the module extracts (i) frequently recurring query patterns and (ii) salient facet names. The query patterns act as priors for the Answerable-QA Generation Agent, guiding it to synthesize answerable questions from node raw data DvD_{v}, while facet names provide optional hints for the Facet Extraction Agent and Summary Agents to emphasize coverage of high-impact attributes during memory construction and tree aggregation. To reduce overfitting, we apply minimum-support thresholds (i.e., only patterns/facets supported by multiple queries are retained); for sensitive production settings, we optionally require human review before deploying updates to the indexing pipeline.

3.7. Lossless Incremental Nearline Indexing

Data freshness is critical for user-facing agents; for example, recruiter memories in LinkedIn’s Hiring Assistant should reflect new interactions within minutes. Full indexing that re-runs all LLM-based summarization and embedding steps is too expensive; incremental updates such as GraphRAG (Edge et al., 2024) are typically lossy and still require periodic full re-indexing.

HLTM natively supports lossless incremental nearline indexing, keeping large-scale memories fresh without full re-indexing. As shown in Figure 4, we maintain a set V⋆V^{\star} of leaf nodes newly created or modified since the last cycle; for each v∈V⋆v\in V^{\star}, we recompute its memory representation MvM_{v} as discussed in Section 3.3, and then update only its ancestor path {u∈V∣v⪯u}\{u\in V\mid v\preceq u\} up to the root. Because each parent is always recomputed from its latest children, the resulting tree is identical to a full rebuild over the latest data snapshot. This enables nearline update windows of a few minutes that are substantially cheaper than full re-indexing while preserving the semantics of a fresh global rebuild.

4. Experiments

4.1. Dataset

We constructed a human-labeled benchmark dataset derived from LinkedIn’s Hiring Assistant usage logs. The dataset spans diverse hiring domains, with gold reference answers curated by domain experts. Each data point contains (i) raw hiring documents, including a recruiter’s historical hiring projects, within-project interactions on candidates, and anonymized candidate and project data; (ii) memory queries issued by the Hiring Assistant, spanning both summary-style queries that aggregate signals across projects to infer preferences (e.g., typical titles, locations, and qualifications) and retrieval-style queries that request targeted projects or evidence snippets for downstream reasoning; and (iii) gold answers, which are personalized to the underlying hiring documents. To improve label reliability, each answer is independently annotated by at least three annotators, and disagreements are resolved via majority voting. Dataset statistics are summarized in Table 1.

4.2. Evaluation Metrics

4.2.1. Performance Metrics

Lexical Similarity Metrics.

Prior work in conversational AI and agent memory evaluation (Chhikara et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026) commonly reports lexical overlap metrics. We report token-level F1 to balance spurious content and missing coverage, and BLEU-1 to provide a complementary, precision-oriented lexical similarity signal.

Semantic Correctness Metrics.

To evaluate answer correctness beyond surface-form overlap, we additionally employ an LLM-as-a-judge score. The judge is given the query, the system-generated answer, and the gold reference answer, and scores factual consistency with the reference by checking key constraints such as numbers and named entities. The judge is instructed to rely only on the gold reference and outputs a scalar score in [0,1][0,1] along with a brief rationale. We validate reliability by measuring agreement between judge ratings and human annotations, observing strong alignment (Cohen’s κ>0.8\kappa>0.8). The full judging prompt is provided in Appendix C.1.

4.2.2. Deployment Metrics

Latency.

We measure both offline indexing latency and online query latency. Offline indexing latency indicates whether a method can refresh and maintain memory at production scale (e.g., millions of documents ingested daily for LinkedIn’s Hiring Assistant). Online query latency directly affects end-user experience in interactive, chat-based workflows. When a method supports parallelism, we run indexing and retrieval with a fixed concurrency setting to reflect realistic deployment conditions.

LLM Invocation Counts and Token Consumption.

We track both LLM call counts and token usage, since together they largely determine serving cost. Our accounting covers all LLM interactions during the query phase, including query rewriting, planning, retrieval-time processing, and final answer generation. We compute token usage with a consistent tokenizer (o200k_base).

4.3. Baselines

To comprehensively evaluate HLTM, we compare against both basic baselines and advanced RAG/memory methods. We hold the backbone LLM and embedding model fixed across methods, and evaluate all systems under the same serving setup and context-window constraints.

4.3.1. Basic Baselines

We include two simple yet strong baselines, following the evaluation practice of Mem0 (Chhikara et al., 2025), to isolate the value of an external memory module. (i) Conventional retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) (Lewis et al., 2020) chunks documents into fixed-length segments (size∈{512,1024,2048}\texttt{size}\in\{512,1024,2048\}), embeds each chunk, and retrieves the top-kk chunks by semantic similarity (k∈{1,3}k\in\{1,3\}) as context for question answering. (ii) Full-context prompting feeds the full available history (or the maximal portion that fits within the LLM context window) directly into the LLM without retrieval or an external store, providing an architecture-free baseline under the same context-length and serving constraints.

4.3.2. Advanced Baselines

We further compare against representative advanced RAG and memory systems that introduce explicit structure beyond flat retrieval. (i) Graph-based methods represent memory as nodes and edges, enabling entity-centric organization and multi-hop retrieval; we include GraphRAG (Edge et al., 2024), HippoRAG (Jimenez Gutierrez et al., 2024), A-Mem (Xu et al., 2025), and SimpleMem (Liu et al., 2026). (ii) Tree-based methods build hierarchical indices via recursive clustering and summarization to balance coverage and retrieval efficiency; we evaluate RAPTOR (Sarthi et al., 2024), and leave TreeRAG (Tao et al., 2025) and MemTree (Rezazadeh et al., 2024) for future comparison once runnable implementations are publicly available. (iii) Other common baselines include ReadAgent (Lee et al., 2024) and Mem0 (Chhikara et al., 2025), which serve as widely used reference points for long-context retrieval and memory-augmented generation.

4.4. Implementation Details

HLTM was originally deployed in LinkedIn’s production environment with PySpark-based offline ingestion and in-house document/vector stores. For this study, we re-implemented HLTM as a standalone Python library for benchmarking. All methods run on Python 3.12 and access LLMs via the Azure OpenAI Service API. We use OpenAI models text-embedding-3-large for embeddings and gpt-4o-mini and GPT-5.2 as representative low-cost and advanced LLMs. We report gpt-4o-mini results in the main paper and include GPT-5.2 results and details in Appendix D. Baselines use default open-source settings unless noted, and all results are averaged over three runs.

4.5. Experiment Result Analysis

4.5.1. Overview

Figure 2 shows that HLTM achieves the best quality–latency trade-off on our benchmark, delivering the highest correctness (0.798) at low query latency (≈\approx3.4 s). Methods with similar latency (e.g., conventional RAG) are substantially less accurate, whereas higher-performing baselines such as HippoRAG (Jimenez Gutierrez et al., 2024) achieve improved correctness only at a substantially higher latency.

4.5.2. Quality Analysis.

Table 2 shows that HLTM outperforms all nine baselines on both query types when using GPT-4o mini. On summary-style queries, HLTM improves Token-F1 and semantic correctness over the strongest baselines (conventional RAG and HippoRAG) by more than 15%22 2 Disclaimer: Results may vary in production environments or with different datasets.. On retrieval-style queries, HLTM achieves the highest F1, exceeding the best baseline (conventional RAG) by more than 10%33 3 Disclaimer: Results may vary in production environments or with different datasets., indicating a favorable precision–recall trade-off. Appendix D.1 (Table 4) reports consistent improvements when using the stronger GPT-5.2 model.

4.5.3. Latency and Cost Analysis.

Figure 5 highlights the trade-off between offline indexing latency and online query latency. HLTM pushes the Pareto frontier by enabling parallel indexing across child nodes and reducing online latency through collapsed-tree retrieval. Token analysis further shows that HLTM reduces query-time token usage by at least 50% relative to graph-based baselines, indicating more efficient context selection and compaction (Table 5 in Appendix D.2).

4.6. Ablation Study and Analysis

We conduct an ablation study to quantify the contributions of tree aggregation, adaptation, and each memory representation. Table 3 shows that disabling tree aggregation (i.e., restricting retrieval to leaf nodes only) causes a large drop in summary-style correctness (0.798→\rightarrow0.678; ≈\approx12 points) and retrieval-style F1 (0.712→\rightarrow0.534; ≈\approx18 points). Figure 6 further verifies this trend across multiple kk values. Removing adaptation also degrades quality (correctness 0.798→\rightarrow0.701; ≈\approx10 points), indicating that aligning aggregation with workload-specific query patterns remains important even when the core hierarchy is intact. Finally, single-representation variants suggest that summary memory contributes most to overall performance, while facet and QA memories provide complementary gains; combining all three yields the best correctness on summary-style queries and the best F1 on retrieval-style queries.

4.7. Hyperparameter Analysis

Figure 6 plots retrieval F1 as a function of the retrieval budget kk. We observe two desirable properties of HLTM. First, performance does not exhibit an early peak: it continues to improve as kk increases, whereas the leaf-only variant peaks and then degrades for larger kk. This suggests that aggregated summaries provide the language model with a structured “navigation map,” reducing confusion from long lists of unstructured leaf-level details when kk is large. Second, HLTM’s curve flattens quickly, indicating weak sensitivity to kk beyond a small threshold. Because bottom-up aggregation has already pooled cross-leaf patterns into higher-level memories, a modest kk recovers most useful information, simplifying hyperparameter tuning and enabling robust deployment with a fixed retrieval budget.

4.8. Privacy Discussion

Privacy is a first-class requirement for production memory systems. In HLTM, isolation is enforced structurally: each node is bound to an identity scope (e.g., recruiter, hiring project), and retrieval is restricted to the subtree rooted at that scope. Recruiter-scoped queries can access only that recruiter node and its owned projects; project-scoped queries are further constrained to a single project. This business-aligned hierarchy lets us index once and query at multiple levels without per-level re-indexing or global LLM routing, while preserving strict privacy isolation.

5. Production Use Case

LinkedIn Hiring Assistant (LiHA) (Gu et al., 2025) is an AI agent for recruiters, powered by LinkedIn’s dynamic talent network, that helps recruiters discover and engage candidates with greater speed and scale. Architecturally, LiHA is a plan-and-execute system centered on a supervisor agent that interprets recruiter intent and orchestrates specialized sub-agents and tools (Figure 7). HLTM is deployed as LiHA’s long-term semantic memory service, providing persistent, context-aware signals to support personalization (Figure 1) and enabling the assistant to adapt recommendations and workflows over time. All memory data remains scoped to the recruiter’s environment and is not used for training content-generating AI models. Customers retain control over their stored memory with robust privacy and management options.

6. Conclusion

We introduce HLTM, a hierarchical, schema-aligned long-term memory framework for industrial LLM agents, and demonstrate its end-to-end deployment in LinkedIn’s Hiring Assistant (Gu et al., 2025). HLTM organizes memories into a tree topology that mirrors real-world business scopes (Section 3.2) and generates memory content via complementary multi-view representations with bottom-up hierarchical aggregation (Sections 3.3–3.4). Experiments on production hiring data show that HLTM consistently outperforms strong RAG and memory baselines by more than 10%44 4 Disclaimer: Results may vary in production environments or with different datasets for the summary-style and retrieval-style queries respectively, while maintaining favorable latency and token cost for real-time, chat-based workflows (Section 4.5). In production, HLTM supports large-scale indexing with freshness guarantees via lossless incremental ingestion (Section 3.7) and provides privacy and observability through business-keyed, transparent nodes (Section 4.8), making it a practical foundation for industrial GenAI products. HLTM is deployed in LinkedIn’s Hiring Assistant to support real recruiter hiring workflows (Section 5). Looking ahead, we plan to extend HLTM to richer cross-entity reasoning, multimodal signals, and additional agent use cases beyond hiring, and to explore tighter integration with agent planners and controllers for end-to-end adaptive systems.
